summary: Computed Rips persistence (H0, H1; ripser) of the (★)-certificate clouds (log u, log B, log C)/log p for 2418 primes p ≡ 1 (4) in [10⁶, 1.2·10⁶], comparing the 100 lowest-R primes (R = 4–8) with the 100 highest (R = 72–82). After regressing each feature on log #points, hard and easy groups do not differ: permutation p = 0.42 (H0 total), 0.27 (H1 total), 0.23 (H1 count) (EVIDENCE). Hard primes have 2–4 unordered certificates, so their 'topology' is just their count; persistence adds no descriptor beyond R(p).

Read BRAINSTORM/prob_lottery_model.md §§3.2–3.4 (compound-Poisson bulk, κ ≈ 3.06, calibrated to the 10⁻⁵ quantile, predicted P(f_II = 0) ≈ exp(−λ/κ)) and DISPROOF_AVENUES.md §4 (zero law −log P(0) ∝ μ^β, β ≈ 0.91, fitted on a ladder of sibling lotteries m/n where zeros are actually observable, then extrapolated with the heavy-tail family in §4.5). A tilted Kubilius sampler would only estimate the tail of a model whose tail is already analytic (Poisson/compound-Poisson). Real-world 'splitting' (conditioning p to kill slices) is DISPROOF_AVENUES §5's adversarial D1–D4 designs at 10¹⁸–10²⁵. The item adds no new test of the real tail.

The repo-status 'untried' is wrong: DISPROOF_AVENUES.md §4.1–4.3 (scripts/z32_ladder.c) already computes Type II failure sets of m/p for m = 4…24, all primes ≤ 10⁸. Failures thin out with m (m = 6: 13, last 2521; m = 8: 21; m = 12: 169; m = 24: still failing at 10⁸). A universal zero law in the cell mean μ, P(f = 0) ≈ exp(−0.535 μ^0.91), is fitted across all m, plus a one-constant crossover law predicting p_last. This is exactly the requested 'expected count vs failure rate across the numerator' threshold picture, at 100× the proposed range.

Classified the repeated-denominator slices exactly (PROVED, two lines). x = y = z is impossible. For 4/p = 2/x + 1/z with p prime, p divides x or z. If z = pk, then (4k−1) | p. If x = pk, then (2k−1) | p and z = (p+1)/4. Both are impossible for p ≡ 1 (mod 4). So every solution at every prime p ≡ 1 (4) has three distinct denominators, while every p ≡ 3 (4) has a repeated one (brute check, primes < 3000: all 218 p ≡ 3 (4) yes, all p ≡ 1 (4) no). The repeated-term slice is empty exactly where ES is hard, so there is nothing to deform.

Literature: Feng (hal-03216035, 2021) proves a DDT arcsine law for divisors in residue classes, but only as a Cesàro mean over n at a fixed modulus. No version exists for the ES coupling (modulus 4C tied to N = 4Cp+1) at a fixed n. Numerics, 300 primes near 10⁶ (9540 certificates): log d/log N for the certificate divisors is a tent peaked at 1/2 (0.23 per decile at 0.4–0.6, 0.016 at the ends), not arcsine. All divisors of the same N do follow the arcsine law (0.147 at the ends). This is forced, not informative: d ≡ d′ ≡ −1 (mod 4C) puts both d and N/d in [4C−1, N/(4C−1)], and mixing over log-harmonic C gives the tent. log C/log p decreases linearly (0.26 in the first decile, 0 in the last), i.e. the known harmonic-in-C mass. The arcsine law only says how the mass inside each window is shaped; it does not point to a better C-range.
